Shareholders,

For the last few weeks we have been building Net Forge, and this week it went from a private project to something any developer, or any AI agent, can pick up and use.

Here is what that means and why we think it matters.

More and more games start as a sentence typed to an AI coding agent. "Make me a co-op survivors game." "Add multiplayer to my three.js scene." The agent picks the tools, writes the code and runs it. So the engine an agent reaches for decides what a lot of people end up building with.

Most game engines were made for people clicking around an editor. Agents can't do that. They work best with code they can read, a typed API they can't misuse, and a way to test what they wrote without a human playing it. Multiplayer makes this harder still, because the server and the browser have to agree on every frame.

Net Forge is built for that from the ground up:

- One game simulation runs the same in the browser and on the server, so multiplayer works from the first line
- A three.js renderer on WebGPU, with a WebGL2 fallback
- Each game's rules live in one typed file an agent can read and safely change
- Playtest bots play the game for you, so an agent can check its own work
- 530 CC0 models and sounds across six art styles, so nothing ships as grey boxes
- Ten complete templates to start from: survivors-like co-op, arena shooter, tower defense, dungeon crawler, idle, platformer, card battler, monster collector, kart racer and party game

What shipped publicly:

- 19 open-source packages on npm published straight from a public repo with npm provenance
- npm create netforge@latest, which turns any template into a running game in about a minute
- An MCP server and a CLI setup command, so Claude, Cursor and other coding agents can drive the engine directly
- Full docs at https://t.co/McEop4isuz, written so both people and AI models can read them, with guides for the questions developers actually ask
- A GitHub template repo for every game, so you can start one with a single click
- Playable demos of the templates on https://t.co/xk9EUOU5rk

Everything public runs with play money. No wallet, no chain, no sign-up.

Why this matters for NetNet: the next step is the Kit, which connects a game to its own token, an in-game store and player rewards. When it goes live, anyone who builds on Net Forge will be able to launch a game with an economy attached in one flow. Each game token will trade against wsNET, so every game that launches adds a new market built on NetNet.

The open engine comes first. The more developers and agents building on it, the more games there are to launch when the Kit arrives.

If you build something, show us. Issues and pull requests are open.

Elon Musk now literally holds the off switch on Anthropic's $2 trillion IPO.

Anthropic's filing shows it has agreed to pay Elon's AI company up to $120.5 billion for computing power. And starting early next year, either side can walk away with 90 days' notice.

The deal is with SpaceXAI, the SpaceX unit that used to be xAI, and it rents Anthropic the Nvidia chips that run Claude.

In May, the price was $1.25 billion a month for one data center in Memphis. Reuters reported the confidential draft of this filing put the total at $84.5 billion. The public version filed today says $120.5 billion.

Once all the capacity arrives in December, the bill jumps: Anthropic expects to pay Musk about $3.1 billion every month.

Anthropic reportedly brought in $16.8 billion last quarter, which works out to about $5.6 billion a month. So more than HALF of what Anthropic earns today is about to go to one supplier.

Now here's where it gets really insane:

The lock-in on those contracts ends in January and March 2027. After that, either side can cancel with 90 days' notice. Fortune reported in July that the clause gives SpaceX a way to take its chips back if Grok suddenly needs more.

Grok competes directly with Claude.

And in February, Elon publicly called Anthropic's AI evil.

So the company selling itself to the public as the safe AI lab is about to run a huge share of its product on hardware owned by its loudest critic. That critic also owns a direct competitor, and he can start the 90-day clock in early 2027.

The filing does warn that some of Anthropic's compute suppliers build their own AI models, and that warning reads very differently once the supplier is Elon.

And Elon needs this deal just as badly: SpaceX's CFO has promised $100 billion in annual revenue by the end of this year. At full speed, Anthropic's rent comes to about $9.3 billion a quarter. That's more than the roughly $7.6 billion SpaceX's entire AI business brought in last quarter.

So 2 of the biggest IPOs in history are now holding each other up, and both of them have a 90-day exit.

Anthropic has a real argument here. Computing power is the scarcest thing in AI right now, and Amazon's cloud capacity for 2027 is reportedly largely sold out. The filing even admits Anthropic badly underestimated how much compute it needed in the past. Grabbing every chip on the market is the rational move, and the same clause lets Anthropic leave if cheaper capacity shows up.

But public buyers deserve 2 things before the listing: Anthropic should publish how much of Claude runs on SpaceX hardware and what happens to its customers if that notice ever arrives. And it should get the 90-day exit removed for the full length of the contract, the same way its other big compute bills are locked in.

Who do they trust to keep Claude running in 2027, Anthropic or Elon Musk?

A few thoughts on agentic video editing I’ve had over the last few days:

1. 99% of ads should be edited agentically now. If your editors are still editing in the timeline, they’re falling behind. I got a message from my senior VE saying that he’s putting out 5x edits/day now at the same quality he was before.

2. The conversation with video editors will be uncomfortable because the timeline is all they’ve ever known. Some will be hesitant and some will be fearful for their job. I think the best way to address this is head on. The tech is inevitable, but having taste is still going to be incredibly valuable to train and give feedback to agents. Those who have this will become more valuable, those who don’t will struggle.

3. Opus 5.5 can natively edit all of your ads without needing any MCPs or plugins. I’ve tried the alternatives and couldn’t find anything that was significantly better than doing everything inside of Claude.

4. Have your senior editor(s) build skills for each style of edit (e.g. mashups, UGC, AI animations…). You can build these by feeding 4-5 inspo edits to Claude and tell it to make a skill out of it. I prefer building lots of mini-skills to one big video editing skill, so that the context stays as relevant as possible.

5. Once you have a base skill (e.g. ugly ads edits), the best way to train it is through feedback loops. Have the skill re-edit the last 25 ads each senior edited then put them in an artifact, and have the senior VE give feedback on each. Keep doing this until the skill is refined and it understands what a good edit is.

6. If you do this, there’s no reason why you shouldn’t be able to make edits that need little/no feedback. Most of ours are approved after v1 or v2, sometimes v3.

7. Only A-player editors should be training the skills.

8. Re adoption in the team, the AI champion builds the v1. Then get out of the way. I’m not the best editor on my team, so my job is to build the harness that lets the best editors train the skills, not build the skills myself.

9. If you want to supercharge this process, have your top editors record their screen as they edit. Turn on Gmeet or loom and get them to narrate the reasoning behind their process. E.g. why they chose this cut, pacing or b-roll clip…this is all context that gets fed into your skills.

10. It takes time to build, train and refine these skills. You have to go through the dip to get out the other side. Budget time in for senior VEs to work on this - otherwise you’ll end up with skills that put out subpar edits and don’t save you much/any time.

11. Operate under the assumption that this is the worst video editing is ever going to be. Opus 5.5 can do most of our editing today…what will Opus 6/Fable 6 be able to do? The editing skills you build are only going to become more valuable as the tech evolves.

I still don’t think people realise how big video editing being unblocked is. Things that I thought were 3-6 months away are now on the table.

Will continue to share more as I learn. CRAZY, crazy times.

I think this story is important because it tells us about the future of cybersecurity (and of course what we can do better at Anthropic). But some of the Washington Post story / reaction on X is wrong. A few corrections:

2115277212824019367.text:
For anyone using Grok Bot or Claude to make video edits, there are a few things nobody seems to be doing.

This is a small clip from an upcoming video of mine.

FIXES: graphics pinned to the screen instead of the scene, dark scenes that break into bands and blocks on X and YouTube, numbers that jiggle while they count, and soft shots that don't match the rest of the edit.

👾Graphics pinned to the screen instead of the scene

The top half of this video has its graphics pinned to the screen the way most edits do, and the bottom half has them locked to the world.

When the camera moves, a label that points at something stays where it was and the picture slides out from under it. NASA Ames tested this with pilots in 1995. Landing in a simulator, they took 2.5 seconds longer to react to a plane on the runway when their flight symbols were on the head-up display instead of the instrument panel. Their explanation was that symbols on the glass don't move the way the world outside does, and that difference pulls attention onto them. Their fix was to draw the symbols as objects in the world so they move with it, and pilots flew their path more accurately.

In an edit, that means tracking how the background moves in each shot, ignoring the people in it, and moving every graphic that points at something along with the camera. A label on a target follows the target, and titles and counters stay fixed.

👾Dark scenes that break into bands and blocks on X and YouTube:

X and YouTube compress what you upload, and the smooth gradients in dark footage turn into bands and blocks. The fix is to smooth those gradients before the grain goes on.

👾Numbers that jiggle while they count:

Counters jiggle because the digits in a lot of fonts are different widths, so the number shifts sideways as it counts. Putting each digit in a fixed-width slot keeps it still.

👾Soft shots that don't match the rest of the edit:

Measure the sharpness of every shot too. The softest one stands out next to the shots around it, and that's the one to regenerate.

2115428485485506783.text:
Big win for local LLM inference!

This open-source engine generates tokens 2.7x faster than Ollama on a MacBook:

I tested it on a base M5 MacBook Pro with Qwen3.5 4B at 4-bit and the same 9.2k-token prompt. Ollama ran its MTP build, so both had speculative decoding.

- Prefill: Ollama 464 tok/s, Magnitude 755 tok/s (1.6x)
- Decode: Ollama 22.6 tok/s, Magnitude 60.0 tok/s (2.7x)
- End to end, Magnitude finished in half the time

The video below shows both runs side by side.

The Ollama numbers don’t mean it’s badly built. Its kernels were simply tuned in advance.

A kernel is the small GPU program behind every matrix multiply and attention step. Its speed depends on choices like how work is split across GPU cores and how data moves through memory.

The best choices change with every chip. Apple Silicon alone spans 8 to 80 GPU cores and under 70 to over 800 GB/s of bandwidth, and every model has its own layer sizes.

A prebuilt engine has to pick one set of settings for all of them, so most local setups run on a compromise.

Magnitude replaces that compromise with tuning on your machine:

↳ When you download a model, it compiles that model’s kernels locally.

↳ It tries different kernel configurations and keeps whichever runs fastest on your chip.

↳ It pairs each model with the fastest speculative decoding drafter it has found, so each pass of the model produces more than one token.

GitHub repo: https://t.co/gpwU34NFlw

(don’t forget to star it 🌟)

This matters most for agents. Every file and tool output has to be processed before the model writes anything, and that prefill step is where kernel efficiency shows up. Concurrent sessions also share prefix caches, so parallel agents don’t slow each other down.

Magnitude is an open-source (Apache 2.0) inference engine written in Rust. It plugs into Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and other agents with one click.

I shared the GitHub repo above.
